title: Flatten a List With Sublists
statement:
Picture a doubly linked list where any node may also have a child pointer to the head of another doubly linked list, and those nodes may have children of their own, like a nested menu.

Flatten it into a single level: each node's child list goes right after that node, before the node's original next node, with the child list itself flattened first. Return the values of the flattened list from head to tail.

Because the tests use plain data, the structure is given as nested arrays: a list is an array of nodes, and each node is [value, childList], where childList is another such array or null. Build real nodes if you like; the reference solutions do, to practise the pointer splice that interviews ask for.

examples.why: Node 2's child list 7 ↔ 8 is spliced in between 2 and 3.
Node 2's own child, 3, goes before 4: a child list is flattened completely before you continue with the parent's next node.

hints: When you meet a node with a child, the child list must be finished before the node's old next comes. What data structure remembers "come back here later"?
Recursively: flatten the child list, splice it between the node and its next, and return the tail so the caller can keep going.
Iteratively: walk the list; when a node has a child, push its next on a stack, link the child in as next, and clear the child pointer. When you fall off the end, pop the stack and link it on.

explain.intuition:
The flat order is a depth-first walk: a node, then everything below it, then its next sibling. The only state you need is the list of next nodes you have postponed, which is exactly a stack (or the call stack, in a recursive version).

The pointer splice for a node cur with a child: save cur.next on the stack, set cur.next = cur.child and child.prev = cur, and clear cur.child. When you reach a node with no next and the stack is not empty, pop the saved node and link it after the current one, fixing its prev. It is the same move as unwrapping a nested DOM fragment in place.
steps: Build the doubly linked nodes from the nested arrays (or take them as given).
Walk with cur from the head, keeping a stack of postponed next nodes.
If cur.child exists: push cur.next if any, link cur.next = cur.child, set cur.next.prev = cur, clear cur.child.
Else if cur.next is null and the stack is not empty: pop nxt, link cur.next = nxt and nxt.prev = cur.
Move cur = cur.next. At the end read the values from the head.
pitfalls: Forgetting to clear child pointers after splicing, which leaves the list looking multilevel.
Forgetting the prev links, so walking backward from the tail gives a different list.
Appending the child list after the parent's whole remaining list instead of right after the parent node.

solutions.title: Recursive pre-order on the nested data
solutions.idea: Visit each node's value, then recurse into its child list before moving on to the next node.

solutions.title: Real nodes, spliced with a stack
solutions.idea: Build the doubly linked structure, then splice each child list in after its parent, postponing the parent's next on a stack.

followups: Do the splice with O(1) extra space: when you meet a child, find the child list's tail and connect it to the parent's next right away.
Undo the flattening: given the flat list and the original depths of each node, rebuild the levels.
